title: Bounded prefetch and debounced tool calls (PRD draft)
body:
Summary:

This is a product-requirements draft that proposes a bounded prefetch and debounced-tool-call model for the Hosted API SDKs and runtime. The intent is to reduce wasted tokens and API calls in low-bandwidth or high-latency clients, provide predictable latency under bursty input, and make structured streaming outputs more stable for downstream tool invocations.

Context and problem statement:

Teams embed Redwood streaming into interactive UIs (mobile chat, IDE assistants, low-power devices) and server-side orchestrators. Two recurring pain points emerge:

1) Over-eager prefetching. SDKs or client orchestrators prefetch model tokens or speculative tool outputs assuming fast networks; when clients are slow or disconnected this wastes tokens and may trigger unnecessary tool invocations, increasing cost and undermining SLAs.

2) Tool-call churn. Models and SDKs may trigger repeated tool calls (search, database queries, function exec) when incremental responses oscillate, or when client acknowledgement is delayed. This causes double-work, race conditions, and increased downstream load.

Goals:

- Provide a bounded prefetch mechanism: SDKs should prefetch up to a configurable token budget per session or per microturn, with soft and hard caps enforced by runtime.
- Debounce tool calls: introduce an adaptive debounce window for tool invocations during streaming, minimizing duplicated calls while preserving responsiveness.
- Deliver deterministic structured frames: ensure that structured outputs used as tool-call inputs are stable across incremental streaming frames (i.e., don’t trigger calls on transient partial parses).
- Maintain latency SLOs: ensure changes do not meaningfully increase 95th/99th percentile latency for interactive flows.
- Expose predictable telemetry: developers and Redwood operators should be able to reason about prefetch budgets consumed, debounced calls prevented, and cost saved.

Non-goals:

- This doc does not attempt to replace the global batching/caching architecture in the runtime. It operates as a client- and session-level control layer plus lightweight runtime guardrails.
- It does not define model-training changes; approach assumes signal availability from inference runtime (partial outputs, commit events).

User personas and flows:

1) Mobile product engineer: cares about battery, bandwidth, and per-session token spend. Wants to limit wasted calls when users background the app.

2) Platform integrator: runs Agents that call internal tools. Wants to avoid duplicate tool-side work and keep downstream services within quotas.

3) SDK maintainer: needs a simple ergonomic API that gives sensible defaults but allows advanced knobs for enterprise customers.

Key concepts and primitives (high level):

- prefetch_budget: integer token budget (soft default 64 tokens per microturn, configurable). SDKs and runtime coordinate this budget per session.

- soft_prefetch_window: time interval (e.g., 150ms) during which the SDK may request additional speculative tokens if client is actively receiving bytes. If the client stalls, speculative tokens are retracted (never committed) and not charged to user.

- hard_prefetch_cap: the maximum speculative tokens allowed across all concurrent streams for an API key to avoid runaway cost.

- debounce_policy: a small adaptive timer for tool invocations. Candidate defaults: 120ms base, exponential backoff up to 2s if streaming is noisy. The timer is reset when a stable structured frame is observed (see below).

- stable_frame_marker: a lightweight frame-level assertion the runtime emits when a structured parse reaches heuristic stability (e.g., JSON schema fields unchanged for N subsequent tokens). Tool callers should only act on frames marked stable.

API / SDK ergonomics (sketch):

- Streaming client change: add an optional session config object when opening streams: {prefetch_budget: 64, debounce: {base_ms: 120, max_ms: 2000}, allow_speculative_tools: true}. Values are strings/numbers in actual SDKs; here we describe behavior.

- Callbacks the SDK exposes: on_speculative_prefetch(tokens_requested, tokens_granted), on_prefetch_retracted(tokens_retracted), on_stable_frame(frame_id, schema_version), on_debounced_call(tool_id, reason). These are optional listeners used by developer apps for logging and UX.

- Tool invocation helper: SDK provides a helper that buffers candidate tool calls and exposes a flush(color=immediate|debounced|on_stable). Default is debounced. Example usage in pseudo-js:

  const session = redwood.openStream({prefetch_budget: 32});
  const call = session.tool('search').input(candidateInput);
  session.maybeFlush(call, {mode: 'debounced'});

Structured streaming and stable frames:

- Problem: partial JSON or schema fragments during streaming cause downstream parsers to think a full payload is available and fire tool calls.

- Proposal: runtime emits continuation metadata with each chunk: {frame_id, tentative_schema_hash, stability_hint}. The SDK only surfaces frames to the developer-level tool invocation surface when stability_hint == STABLE. The stability heuristic is conservative: require two consecutive identical parse trees across non-trivial token slices or an explicit commit token (e.g., newline-delimiter + commit event).

- For low-bandwidth clients, the SDK can optionally surface provisional frames to the app UI but mark them provisional. Only confirmed stable frames will trigger automatic tool calls.

Debounce/backpressure behavior and server-side enforcement:

- The SDK manages local debounce timers. The server-side enforcer in the runtime provides the canonical hard_prefetch_cap and a per-api-key soft budget. If the SDK requests speculative tokens beyond the soft budget, the runtime may return "prefetch_throttled" with a suggested retry window.

- Tool-call de-duplication: the runtime preserves a short-lived idempotency cache for debounced tool calls (per-session id + tool input hash). If the same call is attempted within the debounce window, it returns cached result and increments a telemetry counter. This avoids double execution when debouncing is imperfect.

Observability and telemetry:

Expose the following metrics in Console and per-route telemetry:

- prefetch_budget_consumed (tokens/session), prefetch_retracted (tokens), prefetch_throttles (counts), debounced_tool_calls (counts), tool_call_dedupe_hits (counts), stable_frame_latency_ms (p95).

Dashboard suggestions: a per-application heatmap showing how often debouncing prevented calls and estimated token cost saved.

Compatibility and fallbacks:

- Graceful degradation: if SDK version < X (no prefetch controls), runtime defaults to conservative behavior (no speculative tokens >16) and no automatic debouncing.

- Enterprise override: Dedicated and Private deployments can configure hard_prefetch_cap to be lower/higher depending on contracts.

Rollout plan (phased):

Phase 0 (experiment): wire SDK listeners and runtime telemetry. Expose experimental flags in Console for a small set of customers. Collect telem for 4 weeks.

Phase 1 (opt-in): enable bounded prefetch and debounce by default for mobile SDKs behind a feature flag. Provide migration guides and examples.

Phase 2 (default): flip to on by default for all hosted API keys after measured improvements and low regressions on latency.

Success metrics (signals of improvement):

- 30–60% reduction in speculative token spend for mobile clients (compare cohorts pre/post).
- 40–80% reduction in duplicate downstream tool invocations per session for top 10 customers that reported churn.
- No >5% regression in 95th/99th latency for interactive endpoints.

Open questions and design trade-offs:

- Stability definition: what exact heuristic (token count, parse-id matches, entropy threshold) signals a stable frame? We propose an iterative approach: start with dual-parse equality over sliding window then evaluate false-negative rates.

- Telemetry volume vs privacy: emitting detailed stability traces from every session may be high-volume. Need sampling and PII review.

- UX contract: how should clients visually indicate provisional vs stable content to users? Mobile teams will need design guidance.

Next steps / immediate action items:

1) Engineering spike: implement simple speculative token budget and soft throttle signal in runtime (owner: infra-serving, 2w).
2) SDK spike: add session config + local debounce helper and listeners in JS and mobile SDKs (owner: developer-experience, 2w).
3) Experiment: recruit 3 mid-size customers for opt-in trial and monitor telem (owner: solutions-eng, 4w).
4) Iterate on stability parser heuristics and finalize default debounce parameters.

Appendix: short notes for implementers:

- Prefetch accounting: speculative tokens granted but retracted should not be charged to customer; they should be accounted separately in internal billing logs for visibility.

- Idempotency cache TTL: default 5s per-session to allow quick dedupe without long cache growth.

- Developer docs: include code patterns for immediate flush when user explicitly interacts (tap, submit), bypassing debounce for strong UX cases.

Contact: Marcus Chen (product-hosted-api) for prioritization and experiments.

This draft is intentionally prescriptive at the SDK surface and conservative at runtime enforcement. Feedback requested from serving-runtime, developer-experience SDK owners, and solutions engineering on parameter defaults and rollout cadence.
